defaults.permitted_development: Across Northamptonshire, most dropped-kerb schemes are decided first through the highway authority because the crossing sits within the public highway. That does not guarantee the planning position: access onto a classified road, flats, listed buildings or wider frontage alterations can still mean a planning application is needed.

rules.height_rules: Across Northamptonshire, height is not the main planning test for a dropped kerb, but changes in levels still matter. A scheme can become problematic if raised ground, steep gradients or tall boundary features interfere with safe access.
rules.depth_rules: Across Northamptonshire, the real depth question is practical rather than formula-based: can a vehicle enter and sit inside the site without blocking the footway? Tight front gardens often fail on that point even before wider design issues are considered.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Northamptonshire, the crossing itself stays within the public highway, so utilities, street trees, signs, lighting columns and drainage can all affect the design or lead to refusal. Boundary openings and visibility splays often matter as much as the driveway surface behind the kerb.
rules.roof_rules: Across Northamptonshire, a dropped kerb does not have a roof allowance. The nearest design equivalent is whether the access proposal includes other built elements, such as retaining walls or covered entrance features, which follow separate planning rules.
rules.materials_rules: Across Northamptonshire, the main material choice for a dropped kerb lies behind the crossing, because the authority typically dictates the kerb and footway build specification. Durable, well-drained driveway materials are usually safer than finishes that shed water or fail under turning wheels.

restrictions.conservation_area: A dropped kerb in a conservation area often needs fuller scrutiny if the proposal affects established front boundaries, historic paving or the character of the street.
restrictions.listed_building: Works to form an access for a listed building often need a heritage check as well as highways approval, especially where original frontage features are affected.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or an old planning condition can remove normal householder rights for frontage and access changes, even where the dropped kerb itself still needs separate highway consent.

rules.permitted_development: In West Northamptonshire, creating a new vehicular access usually starts with highway consent rather than a normal householder application. Lowering the kerb and strengthening the footway are public-highway works, and planning permission may still be required if the site fronts a classified road, the property is split into flats, or the proposal depends on larger engineering or boundary changes.

rules.height_rules: There is no normal householder height allowance for a dropped kerb. The practical checks are kerb and driveway levels, gradients, and whether boundary walls, fences or banks have to be reduced to keep safe sightlines.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit, but the access should lead to enough in-curtilage standing space for a vehicle to clear the footway rather than overhang it. Schemes become harder where a car would project onto the pavement or rely on awkward reversing.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and highway issues usually decide a dropped-kerb application more than any householder rulebook. The authority may object because of sightlines, nearby junctions, parking controls, street furniture or conflicts with utility apparatus.
rules.roof_rules: A dropped kerb has no roof-related permitted development test. The nearest equivalent design issue is whether any linked canopy, gate feature or retaining structure is being added as part of the access works, because those elements are assessed under their own rules.
rules.materials_rules: For a dropped kerb, the public-highway build-up is normally specified by the council rather than by the homeowner. On the private side of the boundary, choose surfacing that drains well and will not break up or rut under regular vehicle use.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually makes a new access more sensitive where it removes historic boundary features or changes a traditional frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: If the access serves a listed building or involves curtilage walls, gates, piers or historic paving, listed building consent may be needed as well as any highway or planning approval.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or an old planning condition can remove normal householder rights for frontage and access changes, even where the dropped kerb itself still needs separate highway consent.
